title: Tackling drought: why nature-based solutions are key to a resilient future

content.content: By Oliver Harmar, Natural England's Chief Strategy Officer

This blog explains how climate change is affecting England, with a focus on drought and wildfire, while suggesting the actions that we can take to restore the natural landscapes that protect us and increase our climate resilience.
Drought in England has of course always posed serious challenges for people and the natural world. What's changing is how often we face it.

This year alone the England will have experienced an exceptionally wet winter followed by a long, hot summer bringing about our third drought in five years and the driest July in almost two centuries.

As climate change makes droughts more frequent and severe, the question is no longer just how we respond to the crisis in the moment, but how we adapt for the longer term, as a society, to live in a more unpredictable climate.

It means building landscapes that are naturally more resilient, so they can withstand drought better, recover more quickly afterwards, and reduce the associated risks: wildfire, water shortages, crop loss and biodiversity decline. Nature itself holds many of the answers.
A growing and connected risk

Climate change is driving more frequent droughts and higher wildfire risk, with growing impacts on people, nature and water security. These are not separate challenges. Dry landscapes are fire-prone landscapes, and the two must increasingly be treated as connected risks, requiring cross-sector partnership working to support land managers on the ground.

The scale of what's at stake is significant. For example, In England, 65% of our drinking water comes from surface water such as lakes and rivers, much of it starting out in our upland areas. It means tackling the problem is priority work, for people and nature.
What we're seeing on the ground

Across our National Nature Reserves, drought is affecting water availability in ways that cascade through our landscapes and ecosystems. Ponds, rivers, dykes and wetlands have dried to exceptionally low levels. In some upland sites, species-rich environments have dried out completely, in some cases that may be unprecedented in our records. Lowland raised bogs have seen significant water table declines, particularly where they have not yet been restored, leading to peat breaking down when air reaches it and erosion.

Wildlife has felt these pressures acutely: breeding waders have struggled with reduced feeding opportunities and higher risk of chick dehydration, fish kills have occurred where oxygen levels have dropped, and some specialist wetland invertebrates, including white-faced darter and large heath butterfly populations, have suffered substantial declines.
And farmers are reporting significant reduced yields.

The overall picture is one of significant strain on landscapes that are already contending with multiple, sometimes conflicting, pressures. Some sites this year faced both unusually wet spring conditions and summer drought in the same season, a reminder of just how variable and challenging our climate is becoming.

Fires at sites like Holme Fen in Cambridgeshire illustrate the challenge starkly. Dried peat can burn for months, releasing stored carbon.  They are extremely difficult to extinguish once fire penetrates deep into the ground which also places pressure on our emergency services and people working on those sites to tackle.
Understanding the fuller picture

While the short-term impacts of drought are visible now, there are also impacts that emerge later and recur over time. Natural England is developing a research and monitoring programme specifically focused on the impacts of drought and wildfire, because many of the most serious consequences may not become fully apparent until future seasons.

We are also increasingly responding to drought permits and orders; requests to allow more flexibility in managing water resources when there is an exceptional shortage of rain. These measures are designed to avoid lasting damage, but they are growing in frequency.
Holding water for longer: restoring the systems that protect us
Restoring the natural systems that help our landscapes cope in the first place is critical.

In particular, restoring our wetlands and peatlands so they can do what they naturally would, is one of the most effective tools we have.  It helps them hold onto water for longer to reduce flooding and keep water where it should be helping them resist fire.  Wetter landscapes recover more quickly from drought and help maintain water levels for drinking water as well and water for our treasured wildlife.

Restoration of sphagnum moss on peatland is one of the most common methods.  Restoring this plant cover, alongside work like blocking artificial drainage channels, helps peatlands hold water much more effectively. Long-term restoration work in the Peak District and South Pennines, led by partners such as Moors for the Future, has shown that this kind of restoration can slow the flow of water off the hills, helping to protect communities downstream while also storing carbon and supporting biodiversity. It's a strong example of how work that's good for nature is good for people.

Beavers offer another compelling example. By building dams and creating wetlands, beavers naturally store water, filter it, and help keep the ground moist for much longer after rain has stopped, acting as both a lifeline during drought and a natural firebreak against wildfire.

Reintroducing beavers has real potential to support nature's recovery. Natural England is working closely with partners to manage reintroduction licences carefully, to make sure the return of beavers benefits both wildlife and local communities.
What this means for people
As hotter, drier summers become more common, climate-resilient landscapes play an increasingly important role in protecting people’s health and wellbeing.
Trees, parks, wetlands, rivers and other nature-rich spaces provide cooling shade, help reduce the impacts of heat stress, improve air quality and create places for recreation and relaxation.
As part of our natural health service, they help communities stay healthy, active and resilient in a changing climate.
Working together with the National Drought Group

No single organisation can tackle a challenge of this scale alone. Natural England sits on the National Drought Group. Working alongside government, water companies and other partners to coordinate our response to drought and ensure that the needs of nature are properly represented in national planning.

This collaboration allows us to bring our evidence and experience from reserves across the country into decisions that can improve water management, drought response and long-term resilience planning at a national level.
Looking ahead

On our National Nature Reserves, restored wetlands and bogs have consistently held onto water better than areas that haven't been restored, offering vital refuges for wildlife throughout drought periods. Habitats with more variety and structure, such as developing wooded areas, have proven more resilient than open, exposed habitats.

By continuing to invest in these nature-based solutions, deepening our research into the longer-term impacts of drought and wildfire, and working closely with partners through the National Drought Group and beyond, we can help build a landscape that is genuinely more resilient to the droughts of the future, for wildlife, and for the people who depend on it.

title: RJM International Celebrates Prestigious King’s Award for Enterprise for International Trade

content.content: RJM International has officially been presented with a King’s Award for Enterprise in recognition of its outstanding achievement in International Trade.

On Thursday 10 September 2026, the Lord-Lieutenant of Hampshire, Mr Nigel Atkinson, visited RJM’s headquarters in Winchester to formally present the King’s Award trophy and certificate to Managing Director, John Goldring.

The occasion brought together RJM’s UK-based team, alongside senior colleagues from its operations in the USA and Asia-Pacific. The company was also joined by a number of key suppliers and distinguished guests, including Simon Tufnell, Deputy Lord-Lieutenant of Hampshire; Jamie Scott, Mayor of Winchester; Laura Taylor, Chief Executive of Winchester City Council; and Lucille Thompson, Winchester City Council’s Cabinet Member for Business & Culture.
Recognising International Success

The King’s Award for Enterprise is the UK’s most prestigious business award, recognising companies that demonstrate exceptional achievements across a range of categories. RJM received the award for its sustained success in expanding overseas trade and delivering strong international growth over the past three years.
Reflecting on the achievement, John Goldring, Managing Director of RJM International, said:

“This award is granted to those businesses that have achieved three years’ of consistently strong turnover growth in overseas markets. For us, over the past three years, this has meant good sales in Sweden, Spain, Turkey and Kosovo, as well as further afield in the USA, Malaysia and Australia.

“All of these projects have been quite different, so what this confirms to me is that no matter where in the world a power plant is, and no matter what the combustion technology or the type of fuel, RJM has a viable solution that can help that plant improve efficiency, cut its emissions, raise its MWe output – and increasingly – help it on its transition to net zero.”
The award highlights RJM’s expertise in helping power plants around the world improve performance, reduce emissions and support the transition towards cleaner energy generation.
Celebrating Partnerships and Looking Ahead

Recognising the important role that specialist engineering fabricators play in its international success, RJM invited leading UK and overseas component suppliers to join the celebrations. The event included presentations and workshop sessions designed to share knowledge, strengthen partnerships and discuss future opportunities.
Building on the momentum of this latest achievement, RJM is continuing to focus on expanding its presence in key international markets, including Turkey, the USA, Malaysia and Australia.

The King’s Award for Enterprise is a testament to RJM’s commitment to innovation, engineering excellence and export growth, and reflects the dedication of its employees, partners and customers around the world.
Find out more about RMJ International: RJM International Wins King’s Award for Enterprise 2026

title: What are the symptoms of scarlet fever and is it contagious?

content.content: Scarlet fever is a childhood illness that some might associate with the past, but it remains fairly common in the UK. In recent years, there has been a noticeable increase in cases. Here, we answer the most common questions about scarlet fever, what to look out for and how to reduce its spread.
What is scarlet fever?

Scarlet fever is an infectious disease caused by Streptococcus pyogenes bacteria, otherwise known as group A streptococci (GAS). The same bacteria can also cause illnesses such as strep throat and impetigo, or on rare occasions sepsis. Scarlet fever is defined by a characteristic rash, which develops as a reaction to toxins produced by the bacteria.
Thanks to antibiotics, scarlet fever is now usually a mild illness, but prompt treatment is important to reduce the risk of complications and prevent further spread.
Who gets scarlet fever?

Scarlet fever is mainly a childhood illness. Around 90% of cases occur in children under 10 years old, with the highest rates seen in children aged 2 to 8. Outbreaks can happen in nurseries and schools, where children are in close contact with each other.
Adults can also get scarlet fever, but this is much less common.
Is scarlet fever dangerous in pregnancy?

There is no evidence to suggest that having scarlet fever during pregnancy will harm your baby. However, scarlet fever can make you feel unwell, so it is best to avoid close contact with anyone who has the infection where possible.

If you are pregnant and develop symptoms of scarlet fever, you should contact your GP or NHS 111 promptly for advice. Many of the antibiotics used to treat scarlet fever are safe to take during pregnancy, and early treatment can help you recover more quickly and reduce the risk of complications.
What are the symptoms?
Symptoms often start with a sore throat, fever, headache, nausea and vomiting. After 12 to 48 hours, a distinctive rash usually appears.
The rash:
You can see pictures of the rash on the NHS page for scarlet fever

Other symptoms can include flushed cheeks, swollen glands in the neck and a white coating on the tongue that peels to reveal a red, swollen ‘strawberry tongue’. As the rash fades, the skin may peel, particularly on the fingertips and toes.
Can you have scarlet fever without a rash?

Technically, no. Scarlet fever is defined by the presence of the rash. Group A streptococcal throat infections would be diagnosed as ‘strep throat’ instead. These infections still need medical assessment and antibiotic treatment.
How does scarlet fever spread?

Scarlet fever is highly contagious. The bacteria spread through saliva and mucus, either by close contact with an infected person or via coughs and sneezes. It can also be picked up from contaminated surfaces or shared items such as cups, plates, toys or utensils.
People can pass the infection on before they show symptoms.
What should I do if I think my child has scarlet fever?

If you think you or your child might have scarlet fever, contact your GP practice or NHS 111 as soon as possible. Scarlet fever is usually diagnosed based on symptoms, although a throat swab may be needed.
Early treatment helps children recover more quickly and reduces the chance of serious complications.
How is scarlet fever treated?

Scarlet fever is treated with antibiotics, usually given as a 10-day course. Symptoms often improve within 24 hours, but it is essential to finish the full course to completely clear the bacteria and protect others.
Children and adults with scarlet fever should stay away from nursery, school or work until at least 24 hours after starting antibiotics.
Are there any complications?

Most people recover fully without any problems. However, without treatment, scarlet fever can occasionally lead to complications such as ear infections, sinusitis, throat abscess, cellulitis or pneumonia. More rarely, it can develop into invasive group A strep (iGAS), a serious condition that occurs when the bacteria spread deep into the body.  Parents and carers should seek medical advice if symptoms worsen, do not improve, or if new symptoms appear in the weeks after recovery. Household contacts of scarlet fever cases are at risk of Group A Strep infections, particularly in the 2 to 3 weeks after the scarlet fever was diagnosed, and should seek medical advice if they become unwell.
How can I help prevent the spread?
Good hygiene plays a key role in stopping scarlet fever from spreading:
What is UKHSA’s role?

Scarlet fever is a notifiable disease in England and Wales, meaning suspected cases must be reported to local health protection teams. UKHSA monitors trends in scarlet fever and publishes regular updates on scarlet fever rates in England to help identify outbreaks early and protect communities.
Being aware of symptoms and acting quickly helps keep scarlet fever under control and protects those most at risk.

title: Unlock the MHRA Regulatory Advice Service for Medical Devices

content.content: Do you need help navigating regulatory requirements for a medical device?​

In December 2025, we launched the new MHRA Regulatory Advice Service for medical devices, offering those developing and working with medical devices the opportunity to meet directly with the MHRA regulatory experts.

Since its launch, we have helped companies developing, manufacturing, marketing or distributing medical devices or in vitro diagnostic (IVD) devices understand how UK requirements apply to their specific products.

The service is particularly beneficial for cross-cutting technologies and novel products that have the potential to significantly improve patient outcomes, helping to identify and address regulatory considerations early. Think AI-enabled diagnostics, novel genetic tests and medical device apps to help patients manage their health.
Case study: Virax Biolabs

In February 2026, we held a regulatory advice meeting with Virax Biolabs, a biotechnology company developing a first-of-its-kind IVD test for immune dysfunction in post-acute infection syndromes such as post-acute COVID-19 (also known as long COVID).The company was looking for guidance on how to best establish their intended use statement and validation approach where a reference standard was not available.The MHRA experts provided advice on:
We asked Dr. Nigel McCracken, Chief Operating Officer at Virax Biolabs what advice they would give other companies considering the MHRA regulatory advice service for medical devices:

title: Smart banking: How one trust generated nearly three teachers' worth of additional funding
authors: Louise Davy, Chief Financial Officer, South East Essex Academy Trust

content.content: We had a system that had worked well enough in the past – but recognised times were changing. With eight and soon to be nine schools across primary and secondary phases, the trust was managing multiple individual bank accounts, each requiring separate oversight and administration.

We are a trust that believes in letting schools have autonomy, but with the change in interest rates, it became clear that we were going to be losing out financially by not getting the best returns we could on our bank balances.
The challenge of multiple accounts

Our original structure reflected a common approach across many multi-academy trusts. Each school maintained its own bank account, with head teachers and finance staff responsible for day-to-day banking operations including authorising payroll runs. This created a complex web of financial management that became increasingly inefficient as the trust grew, with plans to reach nine by January 2026.

We have eight schools, which meant 16 people were involved in payroll authorisation because you need two signatories in each school. Add in central payment runs, and we had 18 people involved every month. Now we have just two people handling everything centrally.

Administrative requirements extended beyond just numbers as our central finance team had to track monthly banking tasks for all schools to mitigate potential risks around critical payments like payroll.
The consolidation solution

Our solution came through a systematic consolidation of banking arrangements, moving from individual school accounts to one central account. This wasn't just about simplification – it was about maximising the financial potential of the trust's reserves.

By consolidating everything through one account, we could then put money on deposit relatively easily. We worked closely with our existing bank, whose relationship manager helped us navigate the transition and ensured transaction limits were adjusted to accommodate the larger sums flowing through the central account.

The real difference came when we opened an additional instant saver account with a different bank, offering significantly better interest rates while maintaining the flexibility needed for education funding cycles.

We now move money into this saving account once the DfE funding comes in at the beginning of the month and keep it there until we need it for payments. This means that for most of the month, we're getting a reasonable rate on funds that would otherwise be earning nothing.
Technology enablers
Critical to the success of this transformation was the trust's simultaneous upgrade of our accounting system.

We have moved from individual installations to a centralised system that could handle consolidated banking. We were at the right time in the right place to make that change. Some accounting systems wouldn't support what we've done easily.

SEEAT also implemented automated sweep accounts with the bank. This means funds are automatically moved to higher-interest accounts at the end of each day, further optimising returns without additional administrative burden.
Quantifying success

The financial impact has been substantial. In the 2024-25 academic year, the trust generated £200,0002 in interest on their bank balances – equivalent to funding nearly three additional teachers*. Monthly returns from the saving account alone contribute around £10,000* a month.

When you equate this to almost three teachers, it becomes very real. I acknowledge the 2024-25 return was during a period when interest rates were more favourable and know that the same return may not always be possible every year, but this action will still generate income, that we were not getting under the old system.

This additional income has been reinvested directly into educational provision across all schools in the trust. The central nature of the income allows for strategic deployment of resources. The additional funding was directly reinvested into trust wide education support including leadership expertise for special educational needs assistance, and other pupil-focused resources across all trust schools at a time when such support is increasingly critical.

The process isn't without challenges – changing banks involves complex onboarding procedures that can take months, particularly around trustee verification; banks don’t always understand the education structures to obtain these.

However, the benefits extend well beyond financial returns. Our Head teachers are freed from routine banking administration, allowing them to focus on educational leadership. Central processes are stronger and more resilient. The trust has better oversight of cash flow across all schools.

For trusts considering similar changes, I recommend careful consideration of existing accounting systems and the timing of any consolidation. Would you upgrade your accounting system just to do this? It's expensive, but if you're already planning system changes, building in banking consolidation makes sense.
Looking forward

The trust continues to optimise its approach; we are currently working through the onboarding process with an alternative high street bank to access even better rates. While this involves significant preparation time – ensuring payroll systems can interface with new banking platforms and managing the transition of direct debits – the potential returns justify the investment.
I’ve shared our approach with other academy trusts through the Essex Academies Business Manager Network, helping spread best practice across the region.

For school leaders wrestling with similar challenges around resource optimisation, I believe our approach demonstrates that strategic thinking about seemingly mundane banking arrangements can yield significant benefits for both operational efficiency and educational provision.

Ready to find out more? Visit the DfE's Buying for Schools page to explore the savings platform and banking comparison tool. It costs nothing to take a look, and it could be the best financial decision you make for your school this year.

Any savings, benefits and outcomes described in this case study were provided by Inspire Education Community Trust and reflect its specific experience and circumstances. Individual results will vary between schools and trusts.

title: Do one thing for forests

content.content: Held annually, the Forestry Stewardship Council’s (FSC) Forest Week is a global campaign raising awareness of the importance of sustainable forest management. This year's theme, ‘Do one thing for forests’, is a reminder that practical action matters.

Sustainably managed woodlands deliver far more than timber. They store carbon, support wildlife, manage flood risk, improve air and water quality, and build resilience to a changing climate. Achieving these benefits requires careful, long-term management and, often, collaboration across sectors.
Forestry England: sustainable forestry, certified for the long term

At Forestry England, the most important thing we can do for forests is manage them sustainably. As England's largest supplier of FSC certified round timber, we know that productive forestry and environmental responsibility go hand in hand.
Achieving this requires long-term planning and careful management, with decisions made today shaping forests for generations to come.

By working with standard-setting bodies like the FSC, the UK Woodland Assurance Standard and certification bodies like Soil Association Certification Ltd, we can show that timber is sourced from woodlands where environmental, social and economic considerations are balanced and where management meets recognised standards.

At a commercial scale, best practice means considering the forest as a whole, rather than small parts or projects in isolation. We plan harvesting operations to protect soils and water, create diverse woodland structures, support priority species and establish the next generation of trees. Productive forestry is not simply about producing timber. It is about maintaining healthy, resilient forests that continue to deliver benefits year after year.

For Forestry England, our one thing is our long-term commitment to forest management certification. For over 25 years we’ve been proud to maintain FSC certification, as the trusted and independently verified quality mark of sustainable forest management.
Soil Association: helping more farmers put trees to work on their land
At the Soil Association, our goal is to help more farmers and landowners discover the value of agroforestry.

Agroforestry is the integration of trees into farming systems, alongside crops, livestock or both. While planting trees can often be seen as taking land out of production, our experience shows the opposite can be true. When carefully designed, agroforestry can support productive farming while delivering a range of environmental and financial benefits.

Across the UK, farmers and landowners are adapting to increasing weather extremes, evolving government support schemes and the need to build long-term resilience into their businesses. Many are turning to agroforestry as a practical way to strengthen farm performance while enhancing the natural assets on which farming depends.

Trees can improve soil health, reduce erosion, provide shelter for livestock and crops, support biodiversity and help manage water across the farm. They can also generate additional income through products such as timber, fruit, nuts and biomass, as well as emerging opportunities in nature markets.

The good news is that agroforestry is not a one-size-fits-all approach. From shelterbelts and riparian planting to silvopasture and alley cropping, there are options to suit a wide range of farm types and business objectives.

Our role is to help farmers explore what could work for their land and business. To receive agroforestry news, events and practical guidance from the Soil Association, you can join our network and subscribe to our Trees on Farms newsletter. One tree can make a difference and a well-designed agroforestry system can deliver benefits for generations.
Sylva Foundation and ercol: highlighting the value of home-grown timber

Sylva Foundation and ercol have launched a new collection of furniture demonstrating the value and potential of home-grown timber. Designed by the Sylva Wood School and crafted in limited batches by students on its professional course, the collection showcases how home-grown British timber can be transformed into high-quality, long-lasting furniture while supporting the next generation of makers.

Made from Grown in Britain certified ash, the collection highlights the environmental and economic benefits of sourcing timber from well-managed UK woodlands. Choosing home-grown timber reduces reliance on imports and cuts the carbon emissions associated with transporting timber over long distances.

The collection includes a bookcase, bedside cabinet, side table and curved stool, each hand-finished to celebrate the natural character of British ash and individually numbered. Every piece reflects the skill, care and craftsmanship developed through the Sylva Wood School's hands-on training programme.

For Sylva Foundation, the collaboration is about more than furniture. It demonstrates how education, woodland stewardship and commercial partnerships can work together to increase the use of home-grown timber.

By connecting sustainable woodland management with contemporary design and skilled craftsmanship, the project encourages consumers, makers and woodland owners to recognise the quality, beauty and environmental value of timber grown in Britain. Sales help support Sylva Foundation's ongoing work promoting resilient woodlands, a thriving wood culture and environmental sustainability.
The Tree Council: growing our urban treescapes

Trees and hedgerows in our towns and cities often go unnoticed and underappreciated, yet they form a vital part of healthy, resilient urban places. Recognising urban trees as long-term strategic assets will help us adapt to hotter summers, heavier rainfall and declining biodiversity.

There is growing ambition and investment to plant more urban trees, but creating resilient treescapes requires careful planning. This includes sourcing healthy, diverse, British-grown trees to reduce the risk of introducing new pests and diseases, alongside careful species selection for a changing climate.

Commercial tree nurseries play a vital role in supplying trees at scale. Alongside them, community tree nurseries are making an increasingly important contribution. Often volunteer-led, these groups collect local seeds or take cuttings to grow saplings for planting in their own neighbourhoods. Until recently, little was known about the contribution, yet we estimate they collectively grow more than 400,000 trees every year for local planting projects.

Their benefits extend far beyond producing trees – they connect people with nature, bring communities together and help people develop new skills. By growing trees from locally sourced seed, or trialling future-focused trees species, they help towns adapt to future environmental challenges.

In partnership with M&G plc, Defra and the Community Tree Nursery Collaborative, we are supporting UK communities to establish new tree nurseries and improve existing ones through our Growing Together programme.
RSPB: protecting the legacy of our ancient woodlands

Woodlands are valuable for many reasons, but individual woodlands are better at delivering some objectives than others. Plantation forests are primarily for timber production but support some woodland biodiversity. Ancient woodlands are irreplaceable habitats that should be managed primarily for nature, but, in some cases, may also supply wood as a by-product of active conservation work.

Specialist woodland biodiversity is in decline, making it vital that the woodlands best suited to nature are managed for nature. Guidance on managing ancient woodlands already exists, but if land managers want to do one thing for forests that isn’t often mentioned, they can look beyond the existing borders for space where these woodlands can expand through natural processes.

This isn’t always possible, as adjacent land may be under different ownership, developed into buildings or transport infrastructure (roads and rails), or be a different priority habitat, river or lake. Wherever opportunities do exist, however, managing buffer zones (up to 100 metres wide) to allow seeds from the existing ancient woodland to establish (known as natural colonisation) is excellent practice.

We cannot create new ancient woodlands so natural colonisation at their edges is the next best thing. There are several case studies of woodland creation through natural colonisation to learn from. It requires patient, long-term management, especially of herbivores, but these buffers will help protect our ancient woodlands, and the rare species that depend on them, for generations to come.
Forest Research: adapting for a climate-resilient future

Projections indicate significant shifts in seasonal rainfall, storm and temperature patterns, resulting in more mild and wet winters, and hotter, drier summers. Storms, flooding, heatwaves and droughts are also expected to happen more often and become more severe.

The way we manage forests needs to adapt to the changing climate and increase resilience, so they continue delivering benefits for people and nature. If you’re considering tree planting or woodland creation, it’s essential to consider the risks that climate change poses over the lifetime of the forest and to build resilience into your plans, by adopting climate smart adaptation measures.

The best place to start is the UK Forestry Standard (UKFS). The latest UKFS guidance recommends following the 5-step adaptation framework, a simple management approach ranging from site-level risk assessment through to regular monitoring and evaluation of adaptive practice.

Our Climate Change Hub is the official home of UK forestry climate change guidance, providing information about climate change risks to woodlands and how to address them. The hub signposts to free decision support resources, including the Ecological Site Classification tool, that offer insights into likely future climate shifts and appropriate tree species options, helping you grow resilient trees and make informed woodland creation choices.
Do one thing, together
From certified timber to agroforestry, community-grown saplings to ancient woodland recovery, these 6 contributions show the breadth of practical action being taken across UK forestry today.

Sustainable forest management isn't the responsibility of any one organisation. It depends on farmers, landowners, woodland managers and local authorities each playing their part, guided by recognised standards and long-term thinking.
This FSC Forest Week, we'd encourage you to consider: what's your one thing for forests?

description: For Forestry Stewardship Council’s Forest Week, this blog brings together 6 organisations working across UK forestry, each sharing one practical thing they are doing for forests, from certification and agroforestry to urban treescapes, climate adaptation and timber use.
